```{r}
#|label: setup

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(broom)
library(performance)
library(gt)

data <- attitude |>
  select(rating, complaints, learning, raises)|>
  drop_na()
  
```

### Descriptives Table 

```{r}
#|label: descriptives table 
#|tbl-cap: "Descriptive Statistics for Continuous Variables"

descriptives <- data|>
summarise(
    across(
      c(rating, complaints, learning, raises),
      list(mean = mean, sd = sd, min = min, max = max)
    )
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = c("variable", ".value"),
    names_sep = "_"
  )

descriptives |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = where(is.numeric), decimals = 2)

#Looking at the correlations of data, and specific comparison to the rating 
#cor(data)
#cor(data$rating, data[, c("complaints", "learning","raises")])
```

### Distribution of Ratings 

```{r}
#|label: outcome-distribution 
#|fig-cap: "Distrubtion of ratings across factors"

#Make sure that your table vs figure captions are correctly done, when previewing; titles 

ggplot(data, aes(x = rating)) +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(y = after_stat(density)),
    bins = 13, #change number of bins to see/not the gap - 13 is threshold 
    fill = "#FFC0CB",
    color = "white",
    alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_density(
    linewidth = 0.9,
    color = "#8B636C") +
  labs(
    x = "Overall Workplace Rating",
    y = "Density") +
  theme_light(base_size = 12)
```

### Relationship Between Complaints and Ratings

```{r}
#|label: complaint-ratings scatterplot
#|fig-cap: "Relationship Between Complaints and Ratings"

ggplot(data, aes(x = complaints, y = rating)) + 
  geom_point(alpha = 0.60) +
  geom_smooth(
  method = "lm",
  se = TRUE, 
  colour = "#FFC0CB")+
  labs(
    x = "Handling Employee Complaints",
    y = "Overall Workplace Rating") +
   theme_light(base_size = 12)
```

### Relationship Between Learning and Ratings 

```{r}
#|label: learning-ratings scatterplot 
#|fig-cap: "Relationship Between Opportunity to Learn and Ratings"

ggplot(data, aes(x = learning, y = rating)) + 
  geom_point(alpha = 0.60) +
  geom_smooth(
  method = "lm",
  se = TRUE, 
  colour = "#FFC0CB")+
  labs(
    x = "Opportunity to Learn",
    y = "Overall Workplace Rating") +
   theme_light(base_size = 12)
```

The plots that were generated explored the relationships between the overall workplace rating and the handling of employee complaints, and also the opportunity to learn, respectively. Each plot shows a bivariate relationship to assess whether it may be linear, however it does not control for the other factors/predictors. Both plots maintain a positive relationship that is relatively linear. However, the graph examining workplace rating versus the handling of employee complaints shows observed data points which are closer to the regression line and present a trend that can more confidently be described as linear; the confidence interval band is also smaller reflecting a greater certainty. However, the graph modeling overall ratings versus the opportunity to learn exhibits data that looks more dispersed in its positive trend and maintains more outliers (however, their potential influence has not yet been determined). A greater confidence interval (gray band) can be seen underlying the regression line. 

Before fitting the data, expectation of how the three factors, being handling of employee complaints (complaints), the opportunity to learn (learning), and pay increases (raises), might relate to the workplace ratings. Higher workplace ratings could be assumed to relate to to an improved handling of employee complaints, as it would indicate that the company is attentive towards their employees and aims to resolve any complaints. Therefore, the improved handling of employee complaints, as noted by a higher score would likely be positively correlated with workplace ratings. However, the handling of complaints alone would not be the determining factor of employee ratings, as pay increases might also be a factor in satisfaction as it might be more important to some employees, but additionally a component of the employee complains and how they might be handled. Finally, opportunities for learning can be an additional factor to understanding workplace ratings, as it may be viewed differently throughout individuals - some may enjoy the opportunity to learn and some might not. Their perspective, as well as how they might have brought this issue up in a complaint could furthermore be related and be a significant component in how employees rate their overall experience. 

# Estimating the competing models 

```{r}
#| label: fit-models 

#Intercept-only model 
mod0 <- lm(rating ~ 1, data = data)

#M1: Complaints 
mod1 <- lm(rating ~ complaints, data = data)

#M2: Complaints + Learning 
mod2 <- lm(rating ~ complaints + learning, data = data)

#M3: Expanded 
mod3 <- lm (rating ~ complaints + learning + raises, data = data)
```

# Exploring Models

summary(mod0)
summary(mod1)
summary(mod2)
summary(mod3)

Throughout comparing the complaints coefficient in relation to the employee ratings starting in Model 1 (mod1), the coefficient starts at 0.75, however with the addition of learning in Model 2, the coefficients is decreased to be 0.64. Finally, adjusting for the raises, the coefficients slightly changed to be 0.65. These values can be interpreted as the addition of all variables shows that the positive relationship shows that increased ability to handle employee complaints provides a substantial and positive relationship with the increase of employee ratings. 

# Nested-model F-tests 

```{r}
#|label: nested-model F-tests 

tests <- anova(mod0, mod1, mod2, mod3)

tests
```


```{r}
#|label: table of F-test results 

tests <- tests|>
  select(Res.Df, Df, F, `Pr(>F)`)|>
  rename(
    Residual.Df = Res.Df, 
    Nested.Df = Df,
    Nested.F.Stat = F, 
    Nested.p.Value = `Pr(>F)`
  )

```

## Extracting Model Performance Statistics 
```{r}
#|label: extract model performance 

extracted0 <- glance(mod0)
extracted1 <- glance(mod1)
extracted2 <- glance(mod2)
extracted3 <- glance(mod3)

mods <- c("M0: Null", "M1:Complaints", "M2: + Learning", "M3: + Raises")

extracted.mods <- rbind(extracted0, extracted1, extracted2, extracted3)

```

# Combine Nested Tests & Extracted Model Performance Data
```{r}
#|label: combine-compared-data

comparison.table <- cbind(
  Models = mods,
  extracted.mods, 
  tests)

```

#Calculate Changes in Variance 
```{r}
#| label: create-model-performance-table

comparison.table <- comparison.table|>
    mutate(Delta.R2 = r.squared - lag(r.squared),
    RMSE = c(
      sqrt(mean(residuals(mod0)^2)),
      sqrt(mean(residuals(mod1)^2)),
      sqrt(mean(residuals(mod2)^2)),
      sqrt(mean(residuals(mod3)^2)))
  ) |>
  select(
    Models,
    r.squared,
    Delta.R2,
    adj.r.squared,
    RMSE,
    Residual.Df,
    Nested.Df,
    Nested.F.Stat,
    Nested.p.Value)

```

# Combine and Display Model Comparison Table

```{r}
#|label: combine-model-comparison-table
#|fig-cap: "Model Performance and Nested Model Comparison"

comparison.table|>
  gt()|>
  cols_label(
    Models = "Model",
    r.squared = "R²",
    adj.r.squared = "Adjusted R²", 
    RMSE =  "RMSE", 
    Delta.R2 = "ΔR²", 
    Residual.Df = "Residual Df",
    Nested.Df = "Nested Df", 
    Nested.F.Stat = "Nested F", 
    Nested.p.Value = "Nested p")|>
    fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      r.squared,
      Delta.R2,
      adj.r.squared,
      RMSE,
      Nested.F.Stat),
    decimals = 3) |>
  fmt(
    columns = Nested.p.Value,
    fns = function(x) {
      ifelse(is.na(x),"—", ifelse(x < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", x)))}) |>
  sub_missing(
    columns = c(Delta.R2, Nested.Df, Nested.F.Stat),
    missing_text = "—")

```
